title: Convergence and Accuracy
intro: Sooner or later a simulation stops with 'singular matrix', 'timestep too small' or 'gmin stepping failed'. Most of these come from a handful of causes in the circuit or the models, not from the simulator. This page explains the messages, the options that matter, and a checklist that fixes most cases.

blocks.text: ngspice answers Warning: singular matrix: check node c, then tries gmin stepping and source stepping, which also fail. The cause is topological: a node with no DC path to ground (here the island c-d between two capacitors), a loop of voltage sources or inductors, or a current source in series with a capacitor. Fixes: add a large resistor to ground (1G), set .option rshunt=1e12 to put one on every node, or correct the connection. Check the named node first; with many floating nodes, listing and option node help find them.

items: Look at the circuit: bistable circuits (latches, Schmitt triggers, oscillators) have several or no stable DC solutions. Give .nodeset values or off on a device, or use optran.
Behavioural sources with discontinuities (ternary steps, abs, u()) give Newton nothing smooth to follow: smooth them (tanh instead of a step, a small resistance in series).
Ideal elements in impossible configurations: two voltage sources fighting through a switch with ron=0, a diode across a voltage source with no series resistance. Add realistic resistances.
Models used outside their range, units wrong by 10^6 (W=1 meaning a metre), or a missing .lib corner so a model is undefined.
Options that help: .option gmin=1e-10 (larger minimum conductance), itl1=500 (more iterations), gminsteps and srcsteps (on by default), noopiter (go straight to gmin stepping).

optran: replace the operating point by a short pseudo-transient with ramped sources: optran 0 0 0 100n 10u 0 (skip the plain iteration, gmin and source stepping; 100 ns steps for 10 us). Robust for large circuits, PDK digital blocks and oscillators.

blocks.text: doAnalyses: TRAN: Timestep too small; time = ..., timestep = ...: trouble with node x means the transient could not find a solution at a time point even after reducing the step to its minimum. Usual causes and fixes:

items: A real discontinuity: an ideal switch, a zero rise time, a behavioural source that jumps. Give sources finite edges, switches finite ron/roff ratios (about 1e9 or less), and smooth behavioural expressions.
A node with no capacitance driven by a nonlinear element: a little capacitance (1f to 1p) to ground on high-impedance nodes helps the integration.
Very fast internal events: a smaller tmax so the simulator approaches them gradually.

Tolerances: .option reltol=1e-3 is the default; loosening to 1e-2 sometimes gets past a hard point (check results afterwards); abstol (1e-12 A) may need raising for circuits with large currents (power electronics: abstol=1e-9, vntol=1e-4).
method=gear for stiff circuits and power converters; xmu=0.495 to damp trap ringing that sends Newton astray.
set deltacheck prints the step sizes to show where it struggles; option node lists node numbers to map 'trouble with node 23' to a name.
reltol (default 1e-3): relative tolerance on voltages and currents. 1e-4 for precision work (distortion, offsets); 1e-2 only to get through.
vntol (1e-6 V) and abstol (1e-12 A): absolute tolerances for voltages and currents near zero. Scale them to your circuit: microamp circuits need abstol well below 1e-12, kiloamp circuits much above.
chgtol (1e-14 C) and trtol (7): truncation-error control for transients.
gmin (1e-12 S): conductance added across every junction; raising it helps convergence and adds error.
itl1 (100, DC iterations), itl2 (50, iterations per DC sweep point), itl4 (10, per transient time point), itl6 or srcsteps (source steps).
pivtol and pivrel: matrix pivoting thresholds; rarely needed, sometimes for badly scaled circuits.
temp and tnom, method, maxord, xmu: see Transient Analysis.
klu or sparse: the matrix solver. KLU is faster on large circuits; Sparse is needed for noise and CIDER, and is sometimes faster on small behavioural ones.
1. Run op alone first and read every warning. Fix singular matrices and the named nodes before anything else.
2. Use listing expand to see the netlist ngspice actually built: parameters, units, subcircuit nodes.
3. Replace ideal parts with realistic ones: series resistance on sources and capacitors, finite edges, finite switch resistances, small capacitance on high-impedance nodes.
4. For the operating point: .nodeset, off, larger gmin, optran.
5. For the transient: tmax, method=gear or xmu=0.495, sensible abstol/vntol for the circuit's scale, then reltol as a last resort.
6. Simplify: cut the circuit until it simulates, then add parts back. The part that breaks it is usually the one to look at.
7. Check models: compatibility mode set, the right corner loaded, devices inside their bins and their intended voltage range.

blocks.text: A simulation that runs is not necessarily right. Tighten reltol by ten and compare: if the answer moves, it was not converged in the numerical sense. Check charge conservation in switched-capacitor circuits (behavioural capacitors given as c= rather than q= can create charge), check that an oscillator's amplitude is not set by numerical damping, and check timestep-sensitive quantities (THD, jitter, settling to 0.01%) against a run with a smaller tmax.

blocks.title: Diagnose
blocks.text: A buck converter netlist with ideal switches (ron=0.001, roff=1e12) stops with timestep too small at the first switching edge. Name three changes to try, in order.
solution: Make the switch ratio realistic: ron=10m, roff=1Meg (ratio 1e8), or use a MOSFET model; add a small capacitance across the switch.
Give the gate drive finite edges (10 ns) and set tmax to a fraction of the edge time.
Use method=gear and raise abstol to about 1e-9 for the amp-level currents.
blocks.answer: Realistic switch, finite edges with tmax, then gear and abstol.
